title: Titch and the Upside-Down Map
markdown:
Titch was a goblin with eyes that sparkled like the stars above his home in the Starfall Highlands, where mountains tickled the clouds and the moon painted everything with silver dust. He lived in a snug den between rocky hills, always warm, always safe. With him, always, was Squeaky: a tiny mouse, soft as a dandelion puff, whiskers wiggling at every new smell. Squeaky loved to ride on Titch’s shoulder, peeking from under the cap, a little grey puffball, tiny paws holding tight to the shirt.

One evening, sky rosy pink like a sleepy cheek, Titch had a very important job. Old Farmer Bramble, down in the valley where fluffy white sheep grazed like clouds, had borrowed Titch’s special moon-lantern. Not just any light: shiny silver, glittery glass, catching moonlight and holding it, a soft steady glow, like a little piece of the moon. Titch was to take it back.

Farmer Bramble, jolly, beard as white and fluffy as a dandelion clock, cheeks as red as apples, gave Titch a little rolled-up paper, old and crinkly. “Now, Titch, my boy.” Warm, rumbling like a happy tummy. “Follow this map to my farm. Not too far, but the paths can get twisty, and the shadows like to play games.”

Pointy ears perked. So big, so important. “I will, Farmer Bramble!” Bright as a new penny. Squeaky squeaked, meaning: we’ll find it together.

The moon peeked over the tallest mountain, silvery light, deep friendly shadows that stretched and shrank as if practising. Not far from the den: the Little Silver Forest. Trees with leaves like tiny mirrors, throwing moonlight back in playful twinkles. If you stood still, the twinkles stood still. If you hopped, they hopped too, which Squeaky tested twice. Moss as if sprinkled with diamond dust. Titch almost hummed before he had even started walking, because important jobs, in his experience, deserved a tune.

Titch took a few steps, lantern swinging, a little pool of light around his feet. Squeaky twitched, earthy forest floor. “Squeak! Squeak!” A tiny paw toward moss that glowed brighter than all the rest, as if a piece of the starry sky had fallen there.

“Oh, Squeaky, look!” A happy sigh. A carpet of tiny real stars. Titch stepped just a little off the path. Boots sank into soft damp ground. Fresh earth, sweet wildflowers. Moonlight made dancing patterns. He loved to chase them with his eyes. He was so busy with sparkly moss and peek-a-boo light through the leaves that he forgot Farmer Bramble’s map for a moment.

The map was a very good map, if you looked at it just right. Little pictures of trees and rocks and twisty paths. Titch, in his excitement, had turned it this way and that, trying to match it to the pretty forest. He had even tucked it into his pocket while admiring a big shiny leaf, cool and smooth.

He kept walking, humming a goblin song: “Moonbeam, moonbeam, shine so bright, light my path with all your light.” The path grew smaller. The trees looked jumbled. He pulled the map out. Looked at it, then the trees, then the map. The wiggly line did not look like the trees in front of him at all.

He stopped. A clearing, soft warm light, a tiny cottage like gingerbread and happy wishes. Smoke of warm herbs and baked apples. On a little wooden stool, a woman tending a basket bursting with green leaves and colourful flowers: bright pinks, sunny yellows, deep purples. Kind eyes. A smile that crinkled like a wise old owl. A long flowing scarf the colour of a sunset, dancing even without wind. A kind witch who loved growing things.

She looked up. The lantern made a friendly glow on dewy grass. Squeaky peeked, whiskers wiggling. “Well now.” Leaves on a warm day. “A little goblin and his small friend. You look a bit wobbly. Have you lost your way?”

Goblin cheeks pink as a wild rose. “We were going to Farmer Bramble’s.” He held up the lantern as if it might explain. “But I think the path got all mixed up. Or maybe we did.”

She chuckled, and he felt better. “A little lost. That happens, especially on such a lovely night. And what’s that? A very pretty moon-lantern. Are you collecting pieces of the sky?”

Ears flopping. “No, it’s borrowed. I was taking it back. But my map…” He opened it, sighing.

Her eyes twinkled. “Maps can be tricky. Especially when they’re upside down.” A hand that smelled of mint and lavender. “This is Farmer Bramble’s cottage, yes, but you’ve been walking in circles. The top is the bottom, and the bottom is the top.”

Titch looked at the map, then at her. A happy giggle. “It is upside down!” Squeaky, who had been listening very carefully, gave a loud clear squeak that sounded like: I think she’s right.

She smiled, picked a plump deep-red berry, offered it. “A dreamberry. Sweet dreams. And a little advice: always look twice at your map, and listen to your friends. Sometimes they see things we miss, with sharp eyes and wiggly noses.” She turned the map the right way up. Then, oh, it made sense. A finger that seemed to glow with faint starlight. “Just down that way, past the whispering trees and over the little bubbly stream. You’ll be there soon.”

Titch thanked her with all his heart. Squeaky wiggled. The lantern seemed brighter. The path, with the map the right way up, looked clear. He waved. The Little Silver Forest still sparkled, but now he knew where he was going. Steps steady. Lantern, best friend, a task almost done.

Farmer Bramble’s sheep were still pretending to be clouds. The lantern went home to its nail by the door, still holding a little moon, as lanterns should. Farmer Bramble did not mention circles. He mentioned the dreamberry stain on Titch’s thumb, which counted as proof of a journey. Titch ate the rest of the berry on the way back to the den, and Squeaky claimed the last shiny leaf by sitting on it, which counted as looking twice.
